content.title: Accessibility Is Part of the Interface
content.hook: An interface is not accessible because someone remembered a checklist at the end. It is accessible when people can actually perceive the information, operate the controls, understand what to do, and use the interface with the technology they depend on.
content.context:
People do not all interact with a page in the same way. A person may use a keyboard instead of a mouse. Someone may zoom text. Someone else may use a screen reader, a tool that presents page content aloud or in another accessible form, or have difficulty distinguishing colors. Someone may need simpler wording or clearer instructions.

Accessibility is therefore not a special version of the interface. It is part of the interface.
goals: Understand accessibility as the quality of an interface for people with different ways of seeing, hearing, moving, and processing information.

content.question: A team says: “We will make the page beautiful first, then make it accessible later.” What is the strongest response?

options.text: Accessibility mostly concerns color choices, so it can wait.
Accessibility affects structure, controls, text, focus, and instructions, so it belongs in the design and build process.
Accessibility only matters for government websites.
Accessibility means adding a separate page for people with disabilities.

feedback.correct: Accessibility changes how the interface is structured and operated. Waiting can force you to rebuild parts that should have been accessible from the start.
feedback.incorrect: Accessibility changes how the interface is structured and operated. Waiting can force you to rebuild parts that should have been accessible from the start.

content.title: Four questions to ask
content.text:
For this module, use four plain-language questions:

1. Can the person perceive what matters?

2. Can the person operate the interface?

3. Can the person understand what is happening and what is expected?

4. Can the interface work with the user’s browser and assistive technology?

These questions line up with the four principles in the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG): Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust.

content.question: A form has labels that are unclear, a button cannot be reached by keyboard, and an error is shown only by changing text from gray to red. Which statement is strongest?

options.text: These are three unrelated visual problems.
These are accessibility problems involving understanding, operation, and perceiving information.
Only the color issue is an accessibility problem.
The browser will fix all three automatically.

feedback.correct: Accessibility can fail in different parts of an interaction. The useful move is to ask what the user needs to perceive, operate, or understand.
feedback.incorrect: Accessibility can fail in different parts of an interaction. The useful move is to ask what the user needs to perceive, operate, or understand.

content.title: Tiny audit
content.text: Look at any familiar page you have built before. Without changing anything, name one thing a user must see, one thing a user must operate, and one thing a user must understand to complete the page’s main task.

activities.title: Say it
activities.instruction: Compose your response below, then submit to compare with the reference guide.

content.prompt: Complete: “Accessibility is part of the interface because ______.”
guidelines: State your reasoning clearly in your own words or code.
Compare your response with the reference guide after submitting.
content.sampleResponse:
people with different needs must still be able to perceive, operate, understand, and use the interface.

A strong answer names the user’s ability to use the interface, not merely compliance with a checklist.
